Keep it concrete: name real\n4\ttechnologies and real checks, not placeholders. Length is not quality: prefer one-line table\n5\tcells, cite IDs (V2, Phase 3, E1) instead of restating content, and scale the plan to the system.\n6\tA section with nothing load-bearing is one line (\"None.\", \"N/A — <reason>\"); a section that a\n7\tdeclared exception makes moot is one line citing it.\n8\t\n9\t---\n10\t\n11\t## 1. Classification and constraints\n12\t- **What:** one line on the system.\n13\t- **Type:** software / infra / AI-agentic (or a mix); greenfield or brownfield; small build or not.\n14\t- **Dominant constraint:** correctness | availability | latency | cost | scale | compliance.\n15\t- **Worst failure:** the single failure that would hurt most.\n16\t\n17\t**Budgets** (only the rows that bind; add rows the system needs, such as a cutover freeze window):\n18\t\n19\t| Budget | Target | Label | Checked by |\n20\t|---|---|---|---|\n21\t| Latency | … | REQUIREMENT / BASELINE / ASSUMPTION / UNKNOWN | V… or Phase … |\n22\t| Throughput | … | … | … |\n23\t| Availability / SLO | … | … | … |\n24\t| RPO / RTO | … | … | … |\n25\t| Resource use | … | … | … |\n26\t| AI inference cost | … (AI systems only) | … | … |\n27\t| Storage cost | … | … | … |\n28\t| Operational complexity | … (e.g. services to run, on-call load) | … | … |\n29\t\n30\tAn UNKNOWN target has no number: write the missing input, who supplies it, and the phase that\n31\tneeds it. An ASSUMPTION gives its basis.\n32\t\n33\t**Missing inputs:** the unknowns that would change the plan most, and any assumption the phase\n34\torder rests on.\n35\t\n36\t## 2. Dependency map\n37\tOnly the dependencies that bind and that the phase order does not already show:\n38\t\n39\t| What waits | Depends on | Kind | Blocked from being |\n40\t|---|---|---|---|\n41\t| … | … | decision / validation / risk-security / organizational / economic (structural or runtime only when surprising) | built / deployed / specified / hardened / exposed / committed |\n42\t\n43\tThen one line naming the kinds with no instance (\"No organizational or economic dependencies.\").\n44\tIn brownfield work, mark each dependency CONFIRMED or ASSUMED.\n45\t\n46\t## 3. Tradeoff gates (resolved up front)\n47\t\n48\t| Decision | Reversibility | Default (chosen now) | Assumption | Validated by | Flip condition |\n49\t|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n50\t| Consistency vs availability | R2/R3 + one-clause reason | … | … | V…, a cheap check, or the cited basis | … (for a gated row: \"V… fails, or …\") |\n51\t| Monolith vs services | … | … | … | … | … |\n52\t| Sync vs async | … | … | … | … | … |\n53\t| Build vs buy | … | … | … | … | … |\n54\t| Data-privacy boundary (personal or regulated data) | … | … | … | … | … |\n55\t| <each system-specific R2/R3 decision, e.g. the tenancy model> | … | … | … | … | … |\n56\t| (Brownfield) migration strategy, coexistence and cutover, rollback, system of record | … | … | … | … | … |\n57\t| (AI) prompt+RAG vs fine-tune | … | … | … | … | … |\n58\t| (AI) hosted API vs self-host | … | … | … | … | … |\n59\t\n60\t**R1 defaults:** <decision> → <default>; … (one line; no rows for R1 decisions).\n61\t**N/A:** <considered decisions that do not apply> — <reason> (one line).\n62\tOmit the (Brownfield) and (AI) rows when they do not apply. Inherited brownfield decisions the\n63\tplan will not change are listed once as constraints, not as rows.\n64\t\n65\t## 4. Walking skeleton (Phase 0)\n66\t- The one real request and the real response.\n67\t- Every tier it crosses.\n68\t- How it is deployed, logged, monitored, and rolled back on day zero.\n69\t- Who can reach it (internal or allow-listed traffic behind a flag until its controls exist).\n70\t\n71\tIf an exception changes Phase 0, say so in one line and cite it (E…).\n72\tExit check (V0): a real request succeeds with one trace across every tier; a deploy and a\n73\trollback succeed through the pipeline; an injected failure fires an alert; the first values of\n74\tthe measurable budgets are recorded as baselines, not targets.\n75\t\n76\t## 5. {"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"toolu_bdrk_01SZyTWDGhJdPrQgErQhvXnw","type":"tool_result","content":"1\t# Worked examples: dependencies, validation gates, labels, reversibility, budgets, exceptions\n2\t\n3\tExamples for the rules in `SKILL.md`. This file adds no rules of its own. The tables mix different\n4\tsystems on purpose; they are not one plan.\n5\t\n6\t## 1. Dependency kinds\n7\t\n8\t| Kind | Software | Infra | AI / agentic |\n9\t|---|---|---|---|\n10\t| Structural | invoicing builds on the ledger schema | clusters build on the network + IAM baseline | the retrieval index builds on the chunk schema + metadata |\n11\t| Runtime | the API needs the identity provider up | deploys need DNS and the registry up | the answer path needs the model endpoint and vector store up |\n12\t| Decision | keys, schema, and billing wait on the tenancy model | the credential model waits on pull vs push deploys | the data pipeline waits on prompt+RAG vs fine-tune |\n13\t| Validation | the partitioning scheme waits on \"one primary sustains peak\" | the runner-fleet design waits on \"hosted runners meet the queue-time target\" | answer tuning waits on \"retrieval finds the supporting passage\" |\n14\t| Risk / security | an external beta waits on authorization + tenant isolation | prod admission waits on signed artifacts | agent write access waits on injection containment + a tool allow-list |\n15\t| Organizational | live card payments wait on the acquirer confirming PCI scope | the prod cutover waits on a change-board slot | training on customer data waits on a legal review of data use |\n16\t| Economic | the pricing model waits on payment fees per transaction | the retention policy waits on storage growth | general availability waits on cost per resolved conversation |\n17\t\n18\tCommon misses:\n19\t\n20\t- Treating \"the service starts\" as evidence that it sustains the load.\n21\t- Discovering a lead time (security review, vendor contract, data-processing agreement, production\n22\t  account) in launch week — or, worse, in week one of Phase 0.\n23\t- Scaling an AI feature before cost per resolved conversation is measured on real traffic.\n24\t- Ordering by code imports while a decision is still open, so the code is rewritten when it lands.\n25\t\n26\t## 2. Validation gates\n27\t\n28\tFour independent examples, each from a different system.\n29\t\n30\t| | V1 Capacity (validation) | V2 Retrieval (AI) | V3 PCI scope (risk/security + organizational) | V4 Inference cost (economic) |\n31\t|---|---|---|---|---|\n32\t| **Hypothesis** | One Postgres primary carries the projected write load at the 12-month data size | For answerable questions, the index returns a supporting passage in the top 5 | Card entry only in the provider's hosted fields keeps our PCI DSS scope at SAQ A (reduced, not zero) | Answers cost less per resolved conversation than the human handling they replace |\n33\t| **Method** | Benchmark at 2× projected peak on data sized to the 12-month projection, long enough to include autovacuum and checkpoints | ≥ 200 labeled real questions with known source passages, per index version | Data-flow review against SAQ A eligibility, confirmed with the acquirer or a QSA | Meter cost per turn on shadow traffic, then cost per resolved conversation on a 5% canary for one week |\n34\t| **Acceptance threshold** | p99 commit < 50 ms at 2,000 writes/s (ASSUMPTION: projected peak 1,000 writes/s) | hit rate@5 ≥ 0.90 (ASSUMPTION; about ±4 points of sampling error at 200 questions) | Acquirer or QSA sign-off: no card number is stored, processed, or transmitted by our systems; a PAN scan of logs and databases finds none | UNKNOWN: needs the human cost per ticket from the support lead, before Phase 4 |\n35\t| **Evidence** | Benchmark report stored with the build | Eval report in CI for each index version | Completed SAQ A and attestation of compliance | Cost dashboard export for the canary week |\n36\t| **Unlocks (and if it fails)** | A single-primary data model with sharding deferred; if it fails, the partitioning decision opens | Prompt and answer-format tuning; if it fails, re-chunk or change the embedding model before tuning | Taking live card payments; if it fails, re-scope the card flow | General availability; if it fails, narrow the rollout or route more to humans |\n37\t\n38\tShadow traffic alone cannot measure cost per resolved conversation: users never see the answers,\n39\tso the follow-up turns and resolutions never happen. That is why V4 needs a canary.\n40\t\n41\tA good acceptance threshold:\n42\t\n43\t- is a number with its conditions (load, data shape, duration, sample size) when the property is\n44\t  measured, or a named reviewer's pass/fail sign-off on a stated question when it is a design,\n45\t  security, or legal judgment;\n46\t- carries its label: REQUIREMENT, BASELINE, ASSUMPTION (with its basis), or UNKNOWN (no number);\n47\t- can fail within the phase that owns it, and is wider than its own sampling noise;\n48\t- has a consumer: if nothing downstream changes when it fails, it is an exit check, not a gate.\n49\t\n50\tAnti-patterns:\n51\t\n52\t- **\"Proven because it runs.\"** Running shows the path exists, not that it is fast, safe,\n53\t  correct, or affordable enough.\n54\t- **A number labeled UNKNOWN.** \"99.9% (UNKNOWN)\" is invented precision with a disclaimer. An\n55\t  UNKNOWN has no number.\n56\t- **Validation theater.** Gates on R1 decisions, gates nobody consumes, or a gate for every AI\n57\t  sublayer.\n58\t- **Evidence as a result.** \"Benchmark showed 42 ms\" in a plan written before any benchmark ran.\n59\t- **Evidence that leaks.** A parity or benchmark report that copies regulated records into CI;\n60\t  store identifiers or counts, not the records.\n61\t\n62\t## 3. Reversibility\n63\t\n64\t| Tier | Examples |\n65\t|---|---|\n66\t| **R1** | A library behind an interface, internal naming, log message wording, UI styling, the test runner |\n67\t| **R2** | Queue technology (R3 if it is the system of record and consumers rely on replay), ORM, an internal service boundary, cache topology, the CI system, a structured log schema once alerts or SIEM rules parse it, the UI framework, fine-tuning a model (weeks of data and eval work; a hosted fine-tune is tied to one provider's base model) |\n68\t| **R3** | The data model and identifiers once real data exists, tenancy and isolation, the consistency model, a public API with consumers you cannot update in lockstep, trust boundaries, data residency, data gravity at a vendor, training on customer or personal data (removable only by retraining) |\n69\t\n70\tCost of being wrong: making a storage bucket public is one click to undo, but the exposure cannot\n71\tbe undone, so the change is gated like R3. A cutover with rehearsed reverse replication is cheap to\n72\tundo, but the hour it runs wrong can lose or double-book records, so it is gated as an\n73\tirreversible operation.\n74\t\n75\tBasis instead of a gate: \"One Postgres primary at about 50 writes/s, roughly 100× below a single\n76\tprimary's limits\" needs no benchmark gate; \"standard practice\" alone is not a basis.\n77\t\n78\tSeams that turn R3 into R2 when the plan builds them: expand/contract schema migrations; an\n79\tinterface in front of the vendor's API plus a tested export of your data in an open format; the\n80\traw event log, with a retention policy and per-subject keys if it holds personal data; dual-write\n81\tthrough an outbox or change data capture, with a backfill and a reconciliation check; a tenant ID\n82\ton every row from day one.\n83\t\n84\t## 4. Budgets\n85\t\n86\t| Budget | Target | Label | Checked by |\n87\t|---|---|---|---|\n88\t| Latency | Time to first token p95 < 2 s; complete answer p95 < 6 s | ASSUMPTION: typical for hosted-LLM chat; confirm with the product owner | V0 records the floor; Phase 3 exit check at peak |\n89\t| Throughput | 50 requests/s at peak | REQUIREMENT: stated in the request | Phase 2 load test |\n90\t| Availability / SLO | — | UNKNOWN: needs the availability the business commits to (product owner, before Phase 4); a model API, vector store, and database in series at 99.9% each cap it near 99.7% unless fallback answers count as available | SLIs and burn-rate alerts at Phase 4; attainment over the first 30 days |\n91\t| AI inference cost | — | UNKNOWN: needs the human cost per ticket (support lead, before Phase 4) | V4 |\n92\t| Operational complexity | One service and one managed database; no self-hosted cluster | ASSUMPTION: a two-person team | Phase 3 exit check |\n93\t\n94\tRows that do not bind are left out (here, storage cost). Unknowns are fine; fabricated certainty\n95\tis not. The walking skeleton measures the first real values, and later gates check against them.\n96\t\n97\t## 5. Methodology exceptions\n98\t\n99\t| ID | Rule bypassed | Why it does not apply | Replacement validation | Evidence required | Resumes when |\n100\t|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n101\t| E1 | Walking skeleton first (principle 6) | Feasibility is the main risk: nobody knows whether a model can extract invoice fields accurately enough | Two-week offline spike on 300 labeled invoices covering the vendor and layout mix; proves extraction quality only, so integration and deployment risk stay open | Spike report: accuracy per critical field (total, due date, bank details) and the share of invoices needing no correction (thresholds ASSUMPTION) | The spike passes and Phase 0 builds the production skeleton; if it fails, re-scope or stop |\n102\t| E2 | Skeleton runs in production (principle 6) | Certified medical device: nothing reaches production before clearance | Skeleton runs in a production-equivalent environment on target hardware, under design controls | Verification records traceable into the submission | Permanent for the certified scope: every release passes change control, and a significant change needs re-submission unless an approved change-control plan covers it; uncertified back-office tools follow the normal order |\n103\t| E3 | Dependency order (principle 1) | A regulatory date fixes when the reporting feature ships, before its data source is validated | Build behind a flag against the source's contract, with contract tests, and keep an interim manual report that meets the date | Contract tests pass against the real source, and report totals reconcile with the system of record | The source's validation gate passes; the feature is re-checked before exposure |\n104\t| E4 | Cross-cutting moves in every phase (principle 5) | Throwaway prototype answering one product question in two weeks | Containment instead of hardening: synthetic or consented data only, no production credentials or network path, a separate account, a teardown date | The decision record, and the teardown done or the re-plan started | The prototype is chosen to become a product: re-plan from Step 1 |\n105\t\n106\tNot exceptions:\n107\t\n108\t- \"N/A — <reason>\" for something that does not exist in this system.\n109\t- Brownfield work. Example of the normal method: a CI/CD platform for 50 services takes one real\n110\t  service through the new platform to production in Phase 0, with its old pipeline kept as the\n111\t  fallback, and migrates the rest in waves.\n112\t- Reading principle 6 for software you do not operate: a CLI's skeleton is the released package,\n113\t  installed the way users install it, renaming a real folder in dry-run mode (writes run on a\n114\t  disposable copy until the undo journal's gate passes).\n115\t- Data-protection regimes (HIPAA, PCI DSS, GDPR). This file adds no rules of its own. The tables mix different\nsystems on purpose; they are not one plan.\n\n## 1. Dependency kinds\n\n| Kind | Software | Infra | AI / agentic |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| Structural | invoicing builds on the ledger schema | clusters build on the network + IAM baseline | the retrieval index builds on the chunk schema + metadata |\n| Runtime | the API needs the identity provider up | deploys need DNS and the registry up | the answer path needs the model endpoint and vector store up |\n| Decision | keys, schema, and billing wait on the tenancy model | the credential model waits on pull vs push deploys | the data pipeline waits on prompt+RAG vs fine-tune |\n| Validation | the partitioning scheme waits on \"one primary sustains peak\" | the runner-fleet design waits on \"hosted runners meet the queue-time target\" | answer tuning waits on \"retrieval finds the supporting passage\" |\n| Risk / security | an external beta waits on authorization + tenant isolation | prod admission waits on signed artifacts | agent write access waits on injection containment + a tool allow-list |\n| Organizational | live card payments wait on the acquirer confirming PCI scope | the prod cutover waits on a change-board slot | training on customer data waits on a legal review of data use |\n| Economic | the pricing model waits on payment fees per transaction | the retention policy waits on storage growth | general availability waits on cost per resolved conversation |\n\nCommon misses:\n\n- Treating \"the service starts\" as evidence that it sustains the load.\n- Discovering a lead time (security review, vendor contract, data-processing agreement, production\n  account) in launch week — or, worse, in week one of Phase 0.\n- Scaling an AI feature before cost per resolved conversation is measured on real traffic.\n- Ordering by code imports while a decision is still open, so the code is rewritten when it lands.\n\n## 2. Validation gates\n\nFour independent examples, each from a different system.\n\n| | V1 Capacity (validation) | V2 Retrieval (AI) | V3 PCI scope (risk/security + organizational) | V4 Inference cost (economic) |\n|---|---|---|---|---|\n| **Hypothesis** | One Postgres primary carries the projected write load at the 12-month data size | For answerable questions, the index returns a supporting passage in the top 5 | Card entry only in the provider's hosted fields keeps our PCI DSS scope at SAQ A (reduced, not zero) | Answers cost less per resolved conversation than the human handling they replace |\n| **Method** | Benchmark at 2× projected peak on data sized to the 12-month projection, long enough to include autovacuum and checkpoints | ≥ 200 labeled real questions with known source passages, per index version | Data-flow review against SAQ A eligibility, confirmed with the acquirer or a QSA | Meter cost per turn on shadow traffic, then cost per resolved conversation on a 5% canary for one week |\n| **Acceptance threshold** | p99 commit < 50 ms at 2,000 writes/s (ASSUMPTION: projected peak 1,000 writes/s) | hit rate@5 ≥ 0.90 (ASSUMPTION; about ±4 points of sampling error at 200 questions) | Acquirer or QSA sign-off: no card number is stored, processed, or transmitted by our systems; a PAN scan of logs and databases finds none | UNKNOWN: needs the human cost per ticket from the support lead, before Phase 4 |\n| **Evidence** | Benchmark report stored with the build | Eval report in CI for each index version | Completed SAQ A and attestation of compliance | Cost dashboard export for the canary week |\n| **Unlocks (and if it fails)** | A single-primary data model with sharding deferred; if it fails, the partitioning decision opens | Prompt and answer-format tuning; if it fails, re-chunk or change the embedding model before tuning | Taking live card payments; if it fails, re-scope the card flow | General availability; if it fails, narrow the rollout or route more to humans |\n\nShadow traffic alone cannot measure cost per resolved conversation: users never see the answers,\nso the follow-up turns and resolutions never happen. That is why V4 needs a canary.\n\nA good acceptance threshold:\n\n- is a number with its conditions (load, data shape, duration, sample size) when the property is\n  measured, or a named reviewer's pass/fail sign-off on a stated question when it is a design,\n  security, or legal judgment;\n- carries its label: REQUIREMENT, BASELINE, ASSUMPTION (with its basis), or UNKNOWN (no number);\n- can fail within the phase that owns it, and is wider than its own sampling noise;\n- has a consumer: if nothing downstream changes when it fails, it is an exit check, not a gate.\n\nAnti-patterns:\n\n- **\"Proven because it runs.\"** Running shows the path exists, not that it is fast, safe,\n  correct, or affordable enough.\n- **A number labeled UNKNOWN.** \"99.9% (UNKNOWN)\" is invented precision with a disclaimer. An\n  UNKNOWN has no number.\n- **Validation theater.** Gates on R1 decisions, gates nobody consumes, or a gate for every AI\n  sublayer.\n- **Evidence as a result.** \"Benchmark showed 42 ms\" in a plan written before any benchmark ran.\n- **Evidence that leaks.** A parity or benchmark report that copies regulated records into CI;\n  store identifiers or counts, not the records.\n\n## 3. Reversibility\n\n| Tier | Examples |\n|---|---|\n| **R1** | A library behind an interface, internal naming, log message wording, UI styling, the test runner |\n| **R2** | Queue technology (R3 if it is the system of record and consumers rely on replay), ORM, an internal service boundary, cache topology, the CI system, a structured log schema once alerts or SIEM rules parse it, the UI framework, fine-tuning a model (weeks of data and eval work; a hosted fine-tune is tied to one provider's base model) |\n| **R3** | The data model and identifiers once real data exists, tenancy and isolation, the consistency model, a public API with consumers you cannot update in lockstep, trust boundaries, data residency, data gravity at a vendor, training on customer or personal data (removable only by retraining) |\n\nCost of being wrong: making a storage bucket public is one click to undo, but the exposure cannot\nbe undone, so the change is gated like R3. A cutover with rehearsed reverse replication is cheap to\nundo, but the hour it runs wrong can lose or double-book records, so it is gated as an\nirreversible operation.\n\nBasis instead of a gate: \"One Postgres primary at about 50 writes/s, roughly 100× below a single\nprimary's limits\" needs no benchmark gate; \"standard practice\" alone is not a basis.\n\nSeams that turn R3 into R2 when the plan builds them: expand/contract schema migrations; an\ninterface in front of the vendor's API plus a tested export of your data in an open format; the\nraw event log, with a retention policy and per-subject keys if it holds personal data; dual-write\nthrough an outbox or change data capture, with a backfill and a reconciliation check; a tenant ID\non every row from day one.\n\n## 4. Budgets\n\n| Budget | Target | Label | Checked by |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| Latency | Time to first token p95 < 2 s; complete answer p95 < 6 s | ASSUMPTION: typical for hosted-LLM chat; confirm with the product owner | V0 records the floor; Phase 3 exit check at peak |\n| Throughput | 50 requests/s at peak | REQUIREMENT: stated in the request | Phase 2 load test |\n| Availability / SLO | — | UNKNOWN: needs the availability the business commits to (product owner, before Phase 4); a model API, vector store, and database in series at 99.9% each cap it near 99.7% unless fallback answers count as available | SLIs and burn-rate alerts at Phase 4; attainment over the first 30 days |\n| AI inference cost | — | UNKNOWN: needs the human cost per ticket (support lead, before Phase 4) | V4 |\n| Operational complexity | One service and one managed database; no self-hosted cluster | ASSUMPTION: a two-person team | Phase 3 exit check |\n\nRows that do not bind are left out (here, storage cost). {"type":"assistant","message":{"model":"claude-opus-5-5","id":"msg_bdrk_7kuplnq73qbfbur6kixgv5sbwrldb55sfl7ec4uyfvsojab4hztq","type":"message","role":"assistant","content":[{"type":"text","text":"# BUILD PLAN: Moving the patient scheduling system from on-premises to the cloud with no downtime\n\n## 1. Classification and constraints\n- **What:** Move the hospital's patient scheduling system (app servers, database, batch jobs and interface connections) into a cloud provider without any planned scheduling outage. The data includes patient health information (PHI).\n- **Type:** Infrastructure plus software. It's a change to an existing system, not a new build, and it's large: it handles regulated health data, involves several hard-to-reverse decisions and affects clinics, the call center and outside parties.\n- **Dominant constraint:** Availability, closely followed by correctness. No booking can be lost or doubled.\n- **Worst failure:** During the transition, an appointment is lost, double-booked or silently different between the on-prem and cloud copies. This happens if two databases accept writes at once (\"split brain\") or if a cutover drops transactions. The result is missed or clashing patient care that nobody notices. Gate V6 guards against this.\n\n**Budgets**\n\n| Budget | Target | Label | Checked by |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| Planned scheduling outage | None during the migration | REQUIREMENT (stated in the request) | V6 |\n| Write pause at the database switch | ≤ 30 s, hidden by app retries; reads continue | ASSUMPTION: \"no downtime\" read as \"no failed bookings\". Clinical operations must confirm. | V6 |\n| Workflow latency (slot search, book, reschedule) | p95 ≤ today's p95 + 20% | Today's value is a BASELINE measured in Phase 1. The +20% is an ASSUMPTION (schedulers are on the phone with patients); operations to confirm. | V3, V5 |\n| Throughput | 2× today's peak bookings per minute (Monday-morning call-center surge) | BASELINE (Phase 1) | V5 |\n| Replication lag | p99 < 5 s; never > 60 s | ASSUMPTION: needed to keep the cutover pause short | V4 |\n| Data loss at cutover (RPO) | 0 committed transactions | ASSUMPTION: the only acceptable bar for clinical records; the chief medical information officer (CMIO) to confirm | V6 |\n| Data loss and recovery time after go-live (RPO/RTO) | — | UNKNOWN: the CIO or business-continuity lead supplies it before Phase 1 ends. Today's disaster-recovery figures become the BASELINE. | V7 |\n| Steady-state availability target | — | UNKNOWN: CIO supplies it before Phase 4. Today's uptime becomes the BASELINE in Phase 1. | Phase 5 exit check |\n| Cloud running cost and dual-running cost | — | UNKNOWN: finance supplies the budget before Phase 2 | V5 (sizing), Phase 5 |\n| Coexistence period | ≤ 90 days of running both systems | ASSUMPTION: limits dual cost and on-call load | Phase 5 |\n\n**Missing inputs** (the first two could change the order of phases):\n1. **How the app is built, and who makes it.** I assume a hospital-operated, three-tier system: a browser or thin client, app servers, and one relational database (SQL Server or Oracle). Scheduling messages (HL7 \"SIU\" messages) go through an on-premises interface engine.\n   - If it's a **thick client talking directly to the database**, a new phase is needed before the database move: publish the client through Citrix or virtual desktops near the cloud database.\n   - If it's a **vendor product with a vendor-hosted option**, buying hosting from the vendor may replace most of this plan (see the build-vs-buy line in §3).\n2. **What \"no downtime\" means to clinical operations.** If even a ≤ 30 s write pause is unacceptable, the cutover design is re-planned (see the flip condition on the consistency row in §3).\n3. Database engine, data size and peak volumes. Phase 1 measures these.\n4. Which cloud provider, and whether there is already a landing zone (a pre-configured cloud environment with security guardrails) and a business associate agreement (BAA, the HIPAA contract with the provider).\n5. Whether the schedules include 42 CFR Part 2 substance-use programs or state-protected categories (behavioral health, HIV). If so, access rules and logging get tighter.\n6. Jurisdiction. I assume US and HIPAA; GDPR or state residency laws would add dependencies.\n7. Named people for the cutover go/no-go and decommission approvals.\n\n## 2. Dependency map\n\n| What waits | Depends on | Kind | Blocked from being |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| Phase 0 (any cloud node touching the production network) | BAA covering every service used; a cloud account or landing zone; security architecture review; a change advisory board (CAB) change for the network link (ASSUMED not in hand) | organizational | built / deployed |\n| Full replication of real PHI to the cloud (Phase 2) | PHI controls checked (V2) | risk-security | exposed |\n| Interface repointing and cutover spec | Every consumer of the database and app found: HL7 feeds to the EHR, patient-registration (ADT) feed in, billing, patient portal, SMS/phone reminder vendor, health information exchange (HIE), reporting/data-warehouse ETL, nightly batch jobs, printing, call-center phone integration (all ASSUMED until V1) | validation | specified |\n| Clinic-by-clinic moves in Phase 3 | App ↔ database tolerating the link's round-trip time (V3; ASSUMED) | validation | specified |\n| Third-party feeds (reminder vendor, HIE) after the app moves | Partners adding the new cloud outbound IPs to their allow-lists, which takes weeks (ASSUMED) | organizational | exposed |\n| Running in the cloud database (whether a managed service or VMs) | Vendor support statement and license portability (ASSUMED) | organizational | specified |\n| Database switch (Phase 4) | Dual, diverse private circuits installed, which can take months (ASSUMED not ordered); V4, V5, V6, V7 passed; clinical ops' definition of \"no downtime\" | organizational / validation | committed |\n| Reserved-capacity purchase | Sizing confirmed (V5) and finance budget | economic | committed |\n| Decommissioning on-prem | V8 | risk-security | committed |\n\nAll seven dependency kinds have instances. The structural and runtime ones are already shown by the phase order.\n\n**Inherited constraints** (not changed by this plan):\n- Database engine and schema. Changing them means vendor re-certification and months of work.\n- The HL7 interface engine stays on-prem. Moving it is a separate project.\n- Active Directory remains the identity source.\n- The client application stays as is.\n- Existing paper downtime procedures stay in place.\n\n## 3. Tradeoff gates (resolved up front)\n\n| Decision | Reversibility | Default (chosen now) | Assumption | Validated by | Flip condition |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n| Consistency vs availability | R3: double or lost bookings harm patients | Exactly one writable primary database at all times. Copying is one-way from that primary (the system of record). Never two databases accepting writes. | A short write pause hidden by retries counts as \"no downtime\" | V6, plus clinical ops sign-off on the definition | V6 fails on the pause, or ops rules out any pause → re-plan with the app holding writes in a durable queue during the switch (still one primary) |\n| Migration approach | R2: weeks; vendor certification | Move the app servers unchanged onto cloud VMs. Move the database to a managed service running the same engine. No refactoring. | The vendor supports the managed database; licenses are portable | Vendor statement (Phase 1) and V5 | Vendor won't certify the managed service → same engine on cloud VMs |\n| Which tier moves first | R2: changes the order of waves | App tier first, one clinic at a time, still using the on-prem database. The database primary switches afterwards. | The app's conversation with the database tolerates the link's round-trip time | V3 | V3 fails → app and database move together in one switch (Phase 3 becomes testing on copied traffic only), with an extra V6 rehearsal |\n| Replication mechanism | R2: affects how fidelity and switching work | The database engine's own replication (e.g. SQL Server Managed Instance link or distributed availability group, or Oracle Data Guard). The switch is a role change that also sets up copying back to on-prem. | It works over the hybrid link at the lag target | V4 | V4 fails → a log-based change-capture tool (GoldenGate or the cloud's database migration service) with daily reconciliation |\n| Data-privacy boundary | R3: exposing PHI cannot be undone | One US cloud region. Private connectivity only, no public endpoints. Encryption keys managed by the hospital. Only BAA-covered services. Logs that may contain PHI stay inside the PHI boundary. | Every service the plan needs is BAA-eligible | V2 | A required service isn't covered → replace it, or keep that function on-prem |\n| System of record and rollback during the transition | R3: decides which copy is the truth | On-prem is the system of record until Phase 4. After the switch, the cloud is the system of record, with copying back to on-prem as a warm fallback until V8. | Copying back can be set up right after the switch | V6 (failback rehearsed) | Copying back can't be set up → no cutover |\n| Hybrid connectivity | R2: months of lead time | Two diverse private circuits (ExpressRoute or Direct Connect) plus a site-to-site VPN as backup. Phase 0 runs over the VPN with no real PHI. | Circuits arrive before Phase 4 | V7 | Circuits are late → Phase 4 waits; the date moves, the gate doesn't |\n\n**Low-risk defaults (easy to reverse):**\n- **Build vs buy:** buy. Use the engine's own replication and the hospital's existing monitoring and security log system (SIEM), plus cloud-native monitoring. A vendor-hosted version of the app, if one exists, should be compared before Phase 2.\n- **Infrastructure as code:** Terraform.\n- **Tracing:** OpenTelemetry.\n- **Cutover window:** the lowest-volume window measured in Phase 1. It must avoid month-end and EHR change freezes.\n\n**Not applicable:**\n- Monolith vs services, and sync vs async: no re-architecture during the move. HL7 stays asynchronous through the existing interface engine.\n- AI decisions: there is no AI component.\n\n## 4. Walking skeleton (Phase 0)\n\nPhase 0 is the thinnest real path through every target tier, run once in production with test data before anything else is built.\n\n- **The real request:** An allow-listed IT scheduler, on a hospital workstation, books an appointment for the hospital's designated **test patient** on a **test resource** (e.g. \"ZZTEST CLINIC\", so no real slot is used). The request goes through one cloud app node.\n- **The real response:**\n  - The booking is confirmed.\n  - The HL7 scheduling message reaches the EHR on the test patient's record.\n  - The test rows appear in the cloud database.\n- **Tiers it crosses:**\n  1. Workstation\n  2. Internal cloud load balancer (allow-list)\n  3. Cloud app node (same build as on-prem)\n  4. VPN link\n  5. On-prem primary database (the system of record)\n  6. On-prem interface engine\n  7. EHR\n  8. A filtered change-capture feed carrying only test-patient and test-resource rows\n  9. Cloud database instance (schema only, plus test rows)\n- **Deployed:** Infrastructure via Terraform through the pipeline. The app node image is built from the current release.\n- **Logged:** Logs and traces go to the SIEM and a monitoring workspace inside the PHI boundary.\n- **Monitored:**\n  - A synthetic test-patient booking runs every 5 minutes.\n  - Alerts on link status, replication lag and errors on the app node.\n- **Rolled back:** Remove the node from the load-balancer pool and drop the change-capture feed. The on-prem path is never changed.\n- **Who can reach it:** Only allow-listed IT accounts with MFA. No real PHI reaches cloud storage, because the change-capture filter passes test IDs only. A scan confirms zero rows from other patients. The BAA and security review must be in hand first (§2).\n\n**Exit check (V0):**\n- The test booking succeeds, with one trace across every tier.\n- A deploy and a rollback succeed through the pipeline.\n- Cutting the change-capture feed or the app node fires an alert.\n- First values are recorded as baselines: link round-trip time, booking latency through the cloud node, and lag of the filtered feed. These are a floor measured at near-zero load, not a measure of capacity.\n\n## 5. Phases\n\n- **Phase 1: Discovery, baselines and PHI controls**\n  - **Unlocks:** Real PHI in the cloud (after V2), the choice of which tier moves first (V3), and the cutover spec inputs (V1).\n  - **Depends on:** V0.\n  - **Tasks:**\n    1. Order the circuits if not done already (they have the longest lead time).\n    2. Build the dependency inventory from four sources: 30 days of database connection audits, network flow logs, the interface engine's route list, and the job scheduler. Mark each item CONFIRMED and give it an owner (V1).\n    3. Through the existing change process, add performance monitoring (APM) to the on-prem app. Baseline latency, peak throughput, the lowest-volume window and current recovery figures.\n    4. Run the latency-tolerance test (V3).\n    5. Obtain the vendor's support and licensing statement.\n    6. Get the definitions from clinical ops and the CIO: \"no downtime\", RPO/RTO and availability target.\n    7. Update the HIPAA risk analysis, apply PHI controls and run a penetration test (V2).\n    8. Ask third parties to allow-list the cloud outbound IPs.\n  - **Rollback:** Nothing on-prem changes beyond adding monitoring, which is removed through the change process if needed.\n  - **Exit check:** V1, V2 and V3 pass. The RTO/RPO targets are in hand.\n\n- **Phase 2: Full replica and read-only consumers**\n  - **Unlocks:** Fidelity and capacity evidence, and moving read-only workloads off the on-prem system.\n  - **Depends on:** V2. Starts after V1 is drafted.\n  - **Tasks:**\n    1. Remove the Phase 0 change-capture feed.\n    2. Set up the engine's own replication to the cloud. On-prem remains the system of record; copying runs on-prem → cloud.\n    3. Start daily reconciliation (V4).\n    4. Run the load test on an isolated copy of the database restored inside the PHI boundary (V5).\n    5. Move read-only consumers to the cloud replica one at a time, lowest-risk first (e.g. reporting ETL first, the data warehouse last). Each move is a DNS or connection-string change.\n  - **Rollback:** Point consumers back to on-prem and drop the replica.\n  - **Exit check:**\n    - V4 and V5 pass.\n    - Each moved consumer's output matches its last on-prem run (row counts and totals).\n\n- **Phase 3: App tier in the cloud, one clinic at a time** (if V3 passed)\n  - **Unlocks:** Real users on cloud app nodes before the database switch.\n  - **Depends on:** V3, V1, Phase 2, and third-party allow-listing done.\n  - **Tasks:**\n    1. Scale cloud app nodes into the pool. They still use the on-prem primary.\n    2. Move users in waves by load-balancer weight: IT, then one low-volume clinic, then groups of clinics, then the call center last.\n    3. Repoint any app-originated feeds as each wave goes.\n    4. Copy the batch jobs to the cloud and keep them disabled.\n    5. Run the circuit-failover drill (V7, part 1).\n  - **If V3 failed:** This phase runs copied (\"shadow\") read traffic against the cloud app and replica only. The real move happens in Phase 4.\n  - **Rollback:** Per wave, shift load-balancer weight back to the on-prem nodes. The system of record stays on-prem.\n  - **Exit check:**\n    - Each wave holds p95 latency within budget for 5 business days, compared with the on-prem nodes.\n    - No increase in HL7 errors or backlog.\n\n- **Phase 4: Database primary switch (the cutover)**\n  - **Unlocks:** The cloud becomes the system of record.\n  - **Depends on:** V4, V5, V6 and V7 passed. The circuits are live. Go/no-go sign-off from the named approvers.\n  - **Tasks:**\n    1. Freeze schema changes and pause the batch jobs.\n    2. Confirm replication lag is within threshold.\n    3. Drain writes and switch roles, so the cloud is primary.\n    4. Fence the old primary so it cannot accept writes: set it read-only and revoke the app's write access. Verify a write attempt is rejected.\n    5. Start copying cloud → on-prem.\n    6. Drain the remaining on-prem app nodes.\n    7. Enable the batch jobs in the cloud.\n    8. Run a test booking end to end and reconcile.\n    9. Hold heightened monitoring for 72 h, with downtime procedures staffed on standby.\n  - **Rollback:** The rehearsed failback (switch roles back to on-prem) stays available until V8. The point of no return is decommissioning, not this switch.\n  - **Exit check:**\n    - Reconciliation shows zero mismatches.\n    - Write pause and errors within budget.\n    - All inventory feeds verified flowing.\n\n- **Phase 5: Stabilize and decommission**\n  - **Unlocks:** Exit from the on-prem system and the end of dual-running cost.\n  - **Depends on:** Phase 4. V8 before any destruction.\n  - **Tasks:**\n    1. Run a disaster-recovery test in the cloud: backup restore and a zone failover within the RTO.\n    2. Buy reserved capacity (after V5 and the finance budget).\n    3. Decide whether to keep an on-prem read-only replica for downtime reports (see §10).\n    4. Archive a final backup under the records-retention policy.\n    5. After V8, sanitize media to NIST SP 800-88 and keep the destruction certificate.\n  - **Rollback:** Failback is possible until V8. After V8 there is no rollback; that is the point of no return.\n  - **Exit check:**\n    - V8 passes.\n    - 30 days of availability against the target set in Phase 1.\n\n## 6. Validation gates\n\n| ID | Hypothesis | Method | Acceptance threshold | Evidence | Unlocks (and if it fails) | Phase |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n| V0 | A change can be deployed, observed and rolled back through every tier in production | The test-patient booking from §4 | The V0 exit check in §4 | Trace export, pipeline run logs and alert record in the change ticket | Phase 1 | 0 |\n| V1 | The inventory lists everything that depends on the system | Reconcile 30 days of connection audits and flow logs, interface routes and job-scheduler config against the inventory | Every observed source maps to an entry with an owner and an action; owners sign off. 30 days is an ASSUMPTION meant to cover monthly jobs; quarterly jobs are checked from scheduler config. | Inventory with sign-offs in the IT service-management (ITSM) record | Phase 3/4 specs. If it fails: add items, extend discovery. | 1 |\n| V2 | The PHI controls in the cloud are in place | Configuration scan, penetration test of the hybrid boundary, review of the BAA's service list, updated HIPAA risk analysis (addresses §164.308(a)(1), (b); §164.312(b), (e)) | CISO and privacy officer sign off: no public endpoints on PHI resources; hospital-managed encryption keys; TLS 1.2 or later; audit logs reach the SIEM; no open critical or high pen-test findings | Scan report, pen-test report, risk analysis and signed approval | Phase 2 PHI replication. If it fails: fix and re-test; no PHI in the cloud meanwhile. | 1 |\n| V3 | The app works with the link's round-trip time in its path | Pre-prod clone with 2× the measured round-trip time injected (netem), replaying the top-10 recorded scheduling workflows | Workflow p95 ≤ BASELINE + 20% (ASSUMPTION) | Replay report with database round trips per workflow | Phase 3 clinic waves. If it fails: flip to moving app and database together (§3). | 1 |\n| V4 | The cloud replica is an exact copy and keeps up | Continuous lag metric plus daily row-count and key-range hash reconciliation over 14 days, including month-end and template generation | 0 unexplained mismatches; lag p99 < 5 s and never > 60 s (ASSUMPTION) | Reconciliation reports holding counts and hashes only, no records | Phase 4 spec. If it fails: flip the replication mechanism. | 2 |\n| V5 | The cloud app and database handle peak load | 2-hour load test at 2× peak on an isolated copy, with a batch job running | p95 ≤ BASELINE p95; error rate < 0.1% (ASSUMPTION) | Load-test report and sizing record | Phase 4 and the capacity purchase. If it fails: resize and re-test. | 2 |\n| V6 | The primary can switch with no loss and no double writes, and can fail back | ≥ 2 full rehearsals on a production-sized copy under replayed peak write load, including failback and the fencing test; then the go/no-go checklist on the day | 0 lost or duplicated committed transactions (ASSUMPTION; CMIO confirms); write pause ≤ 30 s (ASSUMPTION); failback ≤ 15 min (ASSUMPTION); 100% of writes to the old primary rejected; sign-off from the named CIO and clinical ops director | Rehearsal logs, reconciliation output, signed go/no-go | Phase 4. If it fails: fix and re-rehearse; there is no date pressure. | starts 3, required before 4 |\n| V7 | Scheduling survives the loss of a circuit or a zone once the cloud is primary | Circuit failover drill (Phase 3); zone failover on a copy; simulated total link loss | Circuit failover with no session loss beyond 60 s (ASSUMPTION); zone failover within the RTO set in Phase 1; downtime reports produced from the on-prem replica | Drill records | Phase 4. If it fails: fix the network or high-availability setup before the switch. | 3 |\n| V8 | Nothing still needs the on-prem system | 30 days with zero connections to the old database or app; clean reconciliation; restore test of cloud backups; final archive verified | 0 connections for 30 consecutive days (ASSUMPTION); a successful restore; sign-off from the CIO, privacy officer and records management | Connection audit, restore report, signed decommission approval | Decommission. If it fails: extend coexistence. | 5 |\n\n## 7. Cross-cutting concerns\n\n| Phase | Security | Observability | Reproducibility | Resilience |\n|---|---|---|---|---|\n| 0 | BAA signed; landing-zone policy blocks public IPs; allow-list plus MFA; secrets in a key vault; change-capture filter keeps PHI out | End-to-end traces; synthetic booking every 5 min; lag, link and error alerts; telemetry classified as PHI | All infrastructure in Terraform, deployed by the pipeline; app image from the release build | On-prem path untouched; rollback = remove from the pool |\n| 1 | HIPAA risk analysis, configuration scanning, pen test (V2); flagging of 42 CFR Part 2 data if present | On-prem baseline dashboards; connection audit and flow logs | Pre-prod clone from code; workflow replay scripts versioned | Second circuit ordered; downtime procedures reviewed against cloud dependence |\n| 2 | Replication over the private link; hospital-managed keys; access reviews; scrubbing of PHI from logs | Lag and reconciliation dashboard; per-consumer metrics | Reconciliation job versioned; replica rebuildable from code | Replica rebuild runbook tested; consumers can be pointed back via DNS |\n| 3 | New outbound IPs allow-listed by partners; internal load balancer and web application firewall (WAF) | Cloud vs on-prem node comparison per wave; synthetic checks per clinic | Same build version on both sides; wave weights as code | Load-balancer weight rollback per wave; circuit failover drill (V7) |\n| 4 | Old primary fenced; credentials rotated; break-glass access logged | Cutover dashboard: write pause, errors, HL7 backlog, reconciliation | Rehearsed, scripted runbook (V6) | Copying back to on-prem; failback rehearsed; downtime procedures staffed |\n| 5 | On-prem accounts and keys retired; media sanitized to NIST SP 800-88 | Burn-rate alerts against the availability target; zero-connection audit (V8) | Final archive restore verified; all cloud changes only through code | Cloud disaster-recovery test against the RTO |\n\n## 8. AI layer\nN/A: there is no AI component.\n\n## 9. Methodology exceptions\nNone.\n\n## 10. Deliberately deferred\n- **Modernizing or refactoring the scheduling app:** pulled forward after V8, as a separate plan.\n- **Moving the interface engine to the cloud:** pulled forward if the hospital decides to leave its on-prem data center.\n- **Cross-region disaster recovery:** pulled forward if the RTO set in Phase 1 requires surviving the loss of a whole region.\n- **A permanent on-prem read-only replica for downtime reports:** decided in Phase 5, and pulled forward if the V7 link-loss drill shows the paper procedures aren't enough.\n- **Autoscaling and cloud-native services instead of the moved VMs:** pulled forward if V5 sizing or finance's cost budget shows the moved VMs are too expensive.\n\nI assumed a three-tier, hospital-operated system under US HIPAA. Classification and constraints\n- **What:** Move the hospital's patient scheduling system (app servers, database, batch jobs and interface connections) into a cloud provider without any planned scheduling outage. The data includes patient health information (PHI).\n- **Type:** Infrastructure plus software. It's a change to an existing system, not a new build, and it's large: it handles regulated health data, involves several hard-to-reverse decisions and affects clinics, the call center and outside parties.\n- **Dominant constraint:** Availability, closely followed by correctness. No booking can be lost or doubled.\n- **Worst failure:** During the transition, an appointment is lost, double-booked or silently different between the on-prem and cloud copies. This happens if two databases accept writes at once (\"split brain\") or if a cutover drops transactions. The result is missed or clashing patient care that nobody notices. Gate V6 guards against this.\n\n**Budgets**\n\n| Budget | Target | Label | Checked by |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| Planned scheduling outage | None during the migration | REQUIREMENT (stated in the request) | V6 |\n| Write pause at the database switch | ≤ 30 s, hidden by app retries; reads continue | ASSUMPTION: \"no downtime\" read as \"no failed bookings\". Clinical operations must confirm. | V6 |\n| Workflow latency (slot search, book, reschedule) | p95 ≤ today's p95 + 20% | Today's value is a BASELINE measured in Phase 1. The +20% is an ASSUMPTION (schedulers are on the phone with patients); operations to confirm. | V3, V5 |\n| Throughput | 2× today's peak bookings per minute (Monday-morning call-center surge) | BASELINE (Phase 1) | V5 |\n| Replication lag | p99 < 5 s; never > 60 s | ASSUMPTION: needed to keep the cutover pause short | V4 |\n| Data loss at cutover (RPO) | 0 committed transactions | ASSUMPTION: the only acceptable bar for clinical records; the chief medical information officer (CMIO) to confirm | V6 |\n| Data loss and recovery time after go-live (RPO/RTO) | — | UNKNOWN: the CIO or business-continuity lead supplies it before Phase 1 ends. Today's disaster-recovery figures become the BASELINE. | V7 |\n| Steady-state availability target | — | UNKNOWN: CIO supplies it before Phase 4. Today's uptime becomes the BASELINE in Phase 1. | Phase 5 exit check |\n| Cloud running cost and dual-running cost | — | UNKNOWN: finance supplies the budget before Phase 2 | V5 (sizing), Phase 5 |\n| Coexistence period | ≤ 90 days of running both systems | ASSUMPTION: limits dual cost and on-call load | Phase 5 |\n\n**Missing inputs** (the first two could change the order of phases):\n1. **How the app is built, and who makes it.** I assume a hospital-operated, three-tier system: a browser or thin client, app servers, and one relational database (SQL Server or Oracle). Scheduling messages (HL7 \"SIU\" messages) go through an on-premises interface engine.\n   - If it's a **thick client talking directly to the database**, a new phase is needed before the database move: publish the client through Citrix or virtual desktops near the cloud database.\n   - If it's a **vendor product with a vendor-hosted option**, buying hosting from the vendor may replace most of this plan (see the build-vs-buy line in §3).\n2. **What \"no downtime\" means to clinical operations.** If even a ≤ 30 s write pause is unacceptable, the cutover design is re-planned (see the flip condition on the consistency row in §3).\n3. Database engine, data size and peak volumes. Phase 1 measures these.\n4. Which cloud provider, and whether there is already a landing zone (a pre-configured cloud environment with security guardrails) and a business associate agreement (BAA, the HIPAA contract with the provider).\n5. Whether the schedules include 42 CFR Part 2 substance-use programs or state-protected categories (behavioral health, HIV). If so, access rules and logging get tighter.\n6. Jurisdiction. I assume US and HIPAA; GDPR or state residency laws would add dependencies.\n7. Named people for the cutover go/no-go and decommission approvals.\n\n## 2. Dependency map\n\n| What waits | Depends on | Kind | Blocked from being |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| Phase 0 (any cloud node touching the production network) | BAA covering every service used; a cloud account or landing zone; security architecture review; a change advisory board (CAB) change for the network link (ASSUMED not in hand) | organizational | built / deployed |\n| Full replication of real PHI to the cloud (Phase 2) | PHI controls checked (V2) | risk-security | exposed |\n| Interface repointing and cutover spec | Every consumer of the database and app found: HL7 feeds to the EHR, patient-registration (ADT) feed in, billing, patient portal, SMS/phone reminder vendor, health information exchange (HIE), reporting/data-warehouse ETL, nightly batch jobs, printing, call-center phone integration (all ASSUMED until V1) | validation | specified |\n| Clinic-by-clinic moves in Phase 3 | App ↔ database tolerating the link's round-trip time (V3; ASSUMED) | validation | specified |\n| Third-party feeds (reminder vendor, HIE) after the app moves | Partners adding the new cloud outbound IPs to their allow-lists, which takes weeks (ASSUMED) | organizational | exposed |\n| Running in the cloud database (whether a managed service or VMs) | Vendor support statement and license portability (ASSUMED) | organizational | specified |\n| Database switch (Phase 4) | Dual, diverse private circuits installed, which can take months (ASSUMED not ordered); V4, V5, V6, V7 passed; clinical ops' definition of \"no downtime\" | organizational / validation | committed |\n| Reserved-capacity purchase | Sizing confirmed (V5) and finance budget | economic | committed |\n| Decommissioning on-prem | V8 | risk-security | committed |\n\nAll seven dependency kinds have instances. The structural and runtime ones are already shown by the phase order.\n\n**Inherited constraints** (not changed by this plan):\n- Database engine and schema. Changing them means vendor re-certification and months of work.\n- The HL7 interface engine stays on-prem. Moving it is a separate project.\n- Active Directory remains the identity source.\n- The client application stays as is.\n- Existing paper downtime procedures stay in place.\n\n## 3. Tradeoff gates (resolved up front)\n\n| Decision | Reversibility | Default (chosen now) | Assumption | Validated by | Flip condition |\n|---|---|---|---|---|---|\n| Consistency vs availability | R3: double or lost bookings harm patients | Exactly one writable primary database at all times. Copying is one-way from that primary (the system of record). Never two databases accepting writes. | A short write pause hidden by retries counts as \"no downtime\" | V6, plus clinical ops sign-off on the definition | V6 fails on the pause, or ops rules out any pause → re-plan with the app holding writes in a durable queue during the switch (still one primary) |\n| Migration approach | R2: weeks; vendor certification | Move the app servers unchanged onto cloud VMs. Move the database to a managed service running the same engine. No refactoring. | The vendor supports the managed database; licenses are portable | Vendor statement (Phase 1) and V5 | Vendor won't certify the managed service → same engine on cloud VMs |\n| Which tier moves first | R2: changes the order of waves | App tier first, one clinic at a time, still using the on-prem database. The database primary switches afterwards. | The app's conversation with the database tolerates the link's round-trip time | V3 | V3 fails → app and database move together in one switch (Phase 3 becomes testing on copied traffic only), with an extra V6 rehearsal |\n| Replication mechanism | R2: affects how fidelity and switching work | The database engine's own replication (e.g. SQL Server Managed Instance link or distributed availability group, or Oracle Data Guard). The switch is a role change that also sets up copying back to on-prem. | It works over the hybrid link at the lag target | V4 | V4 fails → a log-based change-capture tool (GoldenGate or the cloud's database migration service) with daily reconciliation |\n| Data-privacy boundary | R3: exposing PHI cannot be undone | One US cloud region. Private connectivity only, no public endpoints. Encryption keys managed by the hospital. Only BAA-covered services. Logs that may contain PHI stay inside the PHI boundary. | Every service the plan needs is BAA-eligible | V2 | A required service isn't covered → replace it, or keep that function on-prem |\n| System of record and rollback during the transition | R3: decides which copy is the truth | On-prem is the system of record until Phase 4. After the switch, the cloud is the system of record, with copying back to on-prem as a warm fallback until V8. | Copying back can be set up right after the switch | V6 (failback rehearsed) | Copying back can't be set up → no cutover |\n| Hybrid connectivity | R2: months of lead time | Two diverse private circuits (ExpressRoute or Direct Connect) plus a site-to-site VPN as backup. Phase 0 runs over the VPN with no real PHI. | Circuits arrive before Phase 4 | V7 | Circuits are late → Phase 4 waits; the date moves, the gate doesn't |\n\n**Low-risk defaults (easy to reverse):**\n- **Build vs buy:** buy. Use the engine's own replication and the hospital's existing monitoring and security log system (SIEM), plus cloud-native monitoring. A vendor-hosted version of the app, if one exists, should be compared before Phase 2.\n- **Infrastructure as code:** Terraform.\n- **Tracing:** OpenTelemetry.\n- **Cutover window:** the lowest-volume window measured in Phase 1. It must avoid month-end and EHR change freezes.\n\n**Not applicable:**\n- Monolith vs services, and sync vs async: no re-architecture during the move. HL7 stays asynchronous through the existing interface engine.\n- AI decisions: there is no AI component.\n\n## 4. Walking skeleton (Phase 0)\n\nPhase 0 is the thinnest real path through every target tier, run once in production with test data before anything else is built.\n\n- **The real request:** An allow-listed IT scheduler, on a hospital workstation, books an appointment for the hospital's designated **test patient** on a **test resource** (e.g. \"ZZTEST CLINIC\", so no real slot is used). The request goes through one cloud app node.\n- **The real response:**\n  - The booking is confirmed.\n  - The HL7 scheduling message reaches the EHR on the test patient's record.\n  - The test rows appear in the cloud database.\n- **Tiers it crosses:**\n  1. Workstation\n  2. Internal cloud load balancer (allow-list)\n  3. Cloud app node (same build as on-prem)\n  4. VPN link\n  5. On-prem primary database (the system of record)\n  6. On-prem interface engine\n  7. EHR\n  8. A filtered change-capture feed carrying only test-patient and test-resource rows\n  9. Cloud database instance (schema only, plus test rows)\n- **Deployed:** Infrastructure via Terraform through the pipeline. The app node image is built from the current release.\n- **Logged:** Logs and traces go to the SIEM and a monitoring workspace inside the PHI boundary.\n- **Monitored:**\n  - A synthetic test-patient booking runs every 5 minutes.\n  - Alerts on link status, replication lag and errors on the app node.\n- **Rolled back:** Remove the node from the load-balancer pool and drop the change-capture feed. The on-prem path is never changed.\n- **Who can reach it:** Only allow-listed IT accounts with MFA. No real PHI reaches cloud storage, because the change-capture filter passes test IDs only. A scan confirms zero rows from other patients. The BAA and security review must be in hand first (§2).\n\n**Exit check (V0):**\n- The test booking succeeds, with one trace across every tier.\n- A deploy and a rollback succeed through the pipeline.\n- Cutting the change-capture feed or the app node fires an alert.\n- First values are recorded as baselines: link round-trip time, booking latency through the cloud node, and lag of the filtered feed. These are a floor measured at near-zero load, not a measure of capacity.\n\n## 5. Phases\n\n- **Phase 1: Discovery, baselines and PHI controls**\n  - **Unlocks:** Real PHI in the cloud (after V2), the choice of which tier moves first (V3), and the cutover spec inputs (V1).\n  - **Depends on:** V0.\n  - **Tasks:**\n    1. Order the circuits if not done already (they have the longest lead time).\n    2. Build the dependency inventory from four sources: 30 days of database connection audits, network flow logs, the interface engine's route list, and the job scheduler. Mark each item CONFIRMED and give it an owner (V1).\n    3. Through the existing change process, add performance monitoring (APM) to the on-prem app. Baseline latency, peak throughput, the lowest-volume window and current recovery figures.\n    4. Run the latency-tolerance test (V3).\n    5. Obtain the vendor's support and licensing statement.\n    6. Get the definitions from clinical ops and the CIO: \"no downtime\", RPO/RTO and availability target.\n    7. Update the HIPAA risk analysis, apply PHI controls and run a penetration test (V2).\n    8. Ask third parties to allow-list the cloud outbound IPs.\n  - **Rollback:** Nothing on-prem changes beyond adding monitoring, which is removed through the change process if needed.\n  - **Exit check:** V1, V2 and V3 pass. The RTO/RPO targets are in hand.\n\n- **Phase 2: Full replica and read-only consumers**\n  - **Unlocks:** Fidelity and capacity evidence, and moving read-only workloads off the on-prem system.\n  - **Depends on:** V2. Starts after V1 is drafted.\n  - **Tasks:**\n    1. Remove the Phase 0 change-capture feed.\n    2. Set up the engine's own replication to the cloud. On-prem remains the system of record; copying runs on-prem → cloud.\n    3. Start daily reconciliation (V4).\n    4. Run the load test on an isolated copy of the database restored inside the PHI boundary (V5).\n    5. Move read-only consumers to the cloud replica one at a time, lowest-risk first (e.g. reporting ETL first, the data warehouse last). Each move is a DNS or connection-string change.\n  - **Rollback:** Point consumers back to on-prem and drop the replica.\n  - **Exit check:**\n    - V4 and V5 pass.\n    - Each moved consumer's output matches its last on-prem run (row counts and totals).\n\n- **Phase 3: App tier in the cloud, one clinic at a time** (if V3 passed)\n  - **Unlocks:** Real users on cloud app nodes before the database switch.\n  - **Depends on:** V3, V1, Phase 2, and third-party allow-listing done.\n  - **Tasks:**\n    1. Scale cloud app nodes into the pool. They still use the on-prem primary.\n    2. Move users in waves by load-balancer weight: IT, then one low-volume clinic, then groups of clinics, then the call center last.\n    3. Repoint any app-originated feeds as each wave goes.\n    4. Copy the batch jobs to the cloud and keep them disabled.\n    5. Run the circuit-failover drill (V7, part 1).\n  - **If V3 failed:** This phase runs copied (\"shadow\") read traffic against the cloud app and replica only. The real move happens in Phase 4.\n  - **Rollback:** Per wave, shift load-balancer weight back to the on-prem nodes. The system of record stays on-prem.\n  - **Exit check:**\n    - Each wave holds p95 latency within budget for 5 business days, compared with the on-prem nodes.\n    - No increase in HL7 errors or backlog.\n\n- **Phase 4: Database primary switch (the cutover)**\n  - **Unlocks:** The cloud becomes the system of record.\n  - **Depends on:** V4, V5, V6 and V7 passed. The circuits are live. Go/no-go sign-off from the named approvers.\n  - **Tasks:**\n    1. Freeze schema changes and pause the batch jobs.\n    2. Confirm replication lag is within threshold.\n    3. Drain writes and switch roles, so the cloud is primary.\n    4. Fence the old primary so it cannot accept writes: set it read-only and revoke the app's write access. Verify a write attempt is rejected.\n    5. Start copying cloud → on-prem.\n    6. Drain the remaining on-prem app nodes.\n    7. Enable the batch jobs in the cloud.\n    8. Run a test booking end to end and reconcile.\n    9. Hold heightened monitoring for 72 h, with downtime procedures staffed on standby.\n  - **Rollback:** The rehearsed failback (switch roles back to on-prem) stays available until V8. The point of no return is decommissioning, not this switch.\n  - **Exit check:**\n    - Reconciliation shows zero mismatches.\n    - Write pause and errors within budget.\n    - All inventory feeds verified flowing.\n\n- **Phase 5: Stabilize and decommission**\n  - **Unlocks:** Exit from the on-prem system and the end of dual-running cost.\n  - **Depends on:** Phase 4. V8 before any destruction.\n  - **Tasks:**\n    1. Run a disaster-recovery test in the cloud: backup restore and a zone failover within the RTO.\n    2. Buy reserved capacity (after V5 and the finance budget).\n    3. Decide whether to keep an on-prem read-only replica for downtime reports (see §10).\n    4. Archive a final backup under the records-retention policy.\n    5. After V8, sanitize media to NIST SP 800-88 and keep the destruction certificate.\n  - **Rollback:** Failback is possible until V8. After V8 there is no rollback; that is the point of no return.\n  - **Exit check:**\n    - V8 passes.\n    - 30 days of availability against the target set in Phase 1.\n\n## 6.
